in 1824 that specifies limits on the maximum

Carnot's theorem states that all heat engines operating between the same two
thermal or heat reservoirs
cannot have
efficiencies
greater than a
reversible
heat engine operating between the same reservoirs. A
corollary
of this theorem is that every reversible heat engine operating between a pair of heat reservoirs is equally efficient, regardless of the
working substance
employed or the operation details. Since a
Carnot heat engine
is also a reversible engine, the efficiency of all the reversible heat engines is determined as the efficiency of the Carnot heat engine that depends solely on the temperatures of its hot and cold reservoirs.

Carnot's theorem is a consequence of the

. Historically, it was based on contemporary
caloric theory
, and preceded the establishment of the second law.
